data: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory lead)

805 kg at launch (487 kg dry) — X-ray/gamma-ray spectrometer, near-infrared spectrograph, multispectral camera, laser rangefinder (LIDAR), magnetometer. First spacecraft to orbit and land on an asteroid.

© NASA / Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory — public domain. NEAR Shoemaker (Near Earth Asteroid Rendezvous) launched 1996-02-17 from Cape Canaveral on the first of NASA's Discovery-program planetary missions. After an Earth gravity assist (1998-01-23) and a flyby of asteroid 253 Mathilde (1997-06-27), the spacecraft entered orbit around 433 Eros on 2000-02-14 — the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid. Over 12 months of orbital science it returned 160,000+ images and detailed spectral, compositional, and gravitational maps of the S-type chondrite body (~34 km × 11 km × 11 km). On 2001-02-12, after four braking burns from about 26 km, NEAR Shoemaker touched down at 1.9 m/s on Eros just south of the saddle-shaped Himeros, returning images to within about 120 m of the surface — the first soft landing on any small body in the solar system. The spacecraft survived impact and continued transmitting for ~16 days from the surface.

Cape Canaveral, 1996-02-17. First Discovery-program planetary mission. The spacecraft carried five science instruments to perform the first orbital survey of an asteroid.

1997-06-27: NEAR flew within 1,212 km of carbonaceous asteroid 253 Mathilde, returning 500 images of the 50 km body. Largest cratered object ever imaged relative to its size — several giant craters 20–33 km across.

1998-01-23: 540 km Earth flyby, raising the aphelion to match Eros's orbit. The spacecraft was briefly lost after a thruster anomaly aborted its burn of 1998-12-20, 11 months later; NEAR flew past Eros instead and returned 14 months later.

2000-02-14: orbital insertion burn into a 321 × 366 km elliptical orbit around Eros — the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid. Over 12 months, orbit altitude was steadily reduced to build a 35 km near-circular mapping orbit.

2001-02-12: four braking burns brought it down from about 26 km; it touched down at 1.9 m/s. NEAR Shoemaker soft-landed just south of the saddle-shaped Himeros, near 35.7°S, returning images from about 120 m altitude. First soft landing on any small body. The spacecraft survived and transmitted from the surface for ~16 days.
First spacecraft to orbit an asteroid (433 Eros, 2000) and first soft landing on any small body (2001-02-12)

NEAR Shoemaker went to Eros because nobody knew what an asteroid really looked like up close. It arrived to find a world pocked with craters, with a saddle-shaped hollow, covered in fine regolith that had nowhere to go in near-zero gravity. For a year it mapped every ridge and boulder from orbit, then in February 2001 the controllers pressed their luck: they lowered the spacecraft's orbit five times in two weeks, slowed it to walking pace, and set it down on the surface. It survived. For sixteen more days it transmitted from Eros — the first emissary from Earth to rest on a small body.

NASA Discovery-program mission, led by Johns Hopkins University APL. Launched 1996-02-17, NEAR Shoemaker flew past asteroid 253 Mathilde (1997-06-27) before an Earth gravity assist (1998-01-23) phased its orbit to match Eros. Orbital insertion around 433 Eros on 2000-02-14 began a 12-month survey that returned 160,000 images and complete spectral, compositional, and gravitational maps of the 34 × 11 × 11 km S-type body. On 2001-02-12, four braking burns brought the spacecraft down from about 26 km; it touched down at 1.9 m/s in a soft landing just south of the saddle-shaped Himeros, near 35.7°S, returning images to within about 120 m of the surface. The spacecraft survived and transmitted from the surface for ~16 days.
Cape Canaveral, 1996-02-17. First Discovery-program planetary mission.
1997-06-27: 1,212 km flyby of carbonaceous asteroid Mathilde; 500 images.
1998-01-23: 540 km flyby phases the orbit to match Eros.
2000-02-14: first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid; 12 months of orbital science.
2001-02-12: touchdown at 1.9 m/s — first soft landing on any small body.
